explanations.explanation: It’s a signal that a token is the “first‐half” or prefix fragment of a split word (often a proper noun or compound term) – in other words, a marker of a morpheme or subword boundary that cues the model to expect the word’s continuation in the following token.

It appears to be a “boilerplate‐detector” that marks contexts where the text is highly formulaic—in legal or technical/license headers (and similarly structured math/problem statements)—so that the model reliably produces the exact, conventional token (e.g. “two,” “rights,” “express,” “person,” etc.) that belong in those fixed textual fragments.

It appears that this feature signals a “formatting‐or style–switch” cue: when it is active, the model shifts its next-token prediction toward a context‐appropriate, formally delimited or domain‐specific output (for example, producing an em‐dash, a particular punctuation or boilerplate phrase) that fits technical, mathematical, or standardized text. Conversely, without the feature the prediction reverts to a more ordinary continuation.

It appears that this feature is “lighting up” when the model is processing a split‐subword that isn’t a full, stand‐alone word but rather the second (or later) component of a compound or affixed term. In each example, a morpheme (like the “B” of “Epstein‐Barr,” the “F” of “Finder,” the “lat” in “untranslatable,” and so on) is isolated from its base and gains a high activation. In short, the feature marks tokens that serve as the continuation pieces of a split compound (or affix), reflecting the model’s internal representation of word‐part boundaries.
It detects boilerplate header text—structured metadata and comment blocks (including license or copyright notices, generated file info, and notebook JSON keys) that appear at the top of source files.

It signals that the model is “seeing” formal, structured citation or reference formatting—that is, it activates on passages replete with bibliographic metadata and their delimiting punctuation (years, author tokens, brackets, colons, etc.) used to mark citations or legal/documentation references.

This feature detects boilerplate open‐source licensing language—in particular, it signals the transition after phrases like “redistribute it and” where the next token should be “or” in legal license headers.

It flags text that follows a fixed, boilerplate-like template—sections with precise formatting and set phrases (such as legal disclaimers, copyright/version info, timestamps, and call‐to‐action elements) that serve as meta or peripheral content.

It detects a particular subword segment—a morpheme‐ or affix-like piece that appears in the middle or end of a compound or inflected word. In other words, the feature fires when the model is processing a distinct, meaningful sub-part of a longer token (such as a suffix, compound‐boundary element, or specialized name/date fragment) that helps it parse and represent structured, complex words.

It’s a detector for subword “continuation‐tokens”—the signal that a token is not a stand‐alone word but the trailing piece (suffix or inflection) of a split, compound, or morphologically complex word.

This feature detects when a token is only a fragment of a full word—that is, it flags subword segments produced by the tokenizer (often prefixes or “partial‐units”) that will complete into a full term with the following token.

It’s the signal for code‐inclusion syntax—a feature that activates when the text follows the structured, boilerplate patterns of file/header inclusion (e.g. “#include”, angle brackets/quotes, file/path tokens) seen in source code.

It signals situations in which the model’s processing “locks in” an expected next token—that is, the feature “marks” contexts where the output would exactly mirror the baseline (or contrapositive) prediction, preserving verbatim or identity‐consistent tokens (like numbers, common articles, punctuation, or formatted tokens).

It appears that this feature “fires” when the model is in a context of a structured, key‐value or delimited data pattern—a kind of “boundary marker” that cues the expected punctuation or delimiter (often a colon, “x”, underscore, etc.) that separates a label (or key) from its associated content. In short, the feature represents a learned signal for transitions between discrete structured fields in formatted data (or code), so that when it’s strong the model “knows” that a specific punctuation/delimiter token should follow.

It seems this feature fires when the model is processing a sub‐word or non‐initial segment—often the second “piece” of a hyphenated or otherwise split compound (or proper name) that carries much of the content of a multi–token term. In other words, the feature detects and marks the continuation or suffix part in compounds and segmented words, signaling the model’s awareness of morphological boundaries in names, adjectives, and other multiword expressions.
